text: Welcome everyone to the August 16th EEG Meeting. My name is Ian Chen, and I'll be your presenter today.

So let me walk you through the progress we've made over the last two weeks.

First, we conducted a thorough review of the FastICA and t-SNE papers, going through them line by line and working through all the mathematical derivations to really understand the foundational theory.

Second, we worked on IC clustering from the ICA encoder pipeline, specifically checking how well the ICA alignment performs on regression tasks.

Third, we found that replacing the encoder with a full MLP architecture actually shows competitive results, which is quite promising.

Fourth, we've been trying to use EEGNet to encode components crossed with time EEG data to see if that improves our approach.

And finally, we've been investigating the memorization problem of the encoder, which is an important issue we need to address moving forward.

Let me walk you through our experimental protocol. The timeline shows how each trial is structured.

We begin with a fixation cross presented for one thousand milliseconds. This is followed by our first stimulus, S1, which lasts two thousand milliseconds and displays a parabolic function. After S1, there's an interstimulus interval, or ISI, of one thousand milliseconds.

Next comes our second stimulus, S2, highlighted here in blue, which is presented for five thousand milliseconds. This is a fixed two-second EEG length recording window. S2 shows the equation y equals x squared. Following S2, there's another ISI of one thousand milliseconds.

Now, looking at our trigger codes: At the start, we send trigger eleven for trials with the correct equation, and trigger ten for trials with an incorrect equation. During the S2 presentation phase, we send triggers sixty-one through one-twenty, which correspond to the various questions being presented. Finally, at the end of the trial, we send trigger two-oh-one when the participant answers correctly, and trigger two hundred when they answer incorrectly.

Let me walk you through our preprocessing pipeline. First, we apply a notch filter at 60 Hertz to remove line noise. Second, we use a bandpass filter from 0.1 to 40 Hertz. Third, we average reference the data. Fourth, we perform ICA ocular artifact removal to clean up eye movement contamination. 

In step five, we extract epochs from negative 0.2 to 2.0 seconds, with a baseline correction applied from negative 0.2 to 0 seconds. For step six, we set a rejection threshold of 150 microvolts peak-to-peak, which automatically drops any epoch exceeding this value. It's important to note that the number of epochs retained varies across subjects. In step seven, each surviving epoch is tagged as either 1 for correct trials—corresponding to event code 201—or 0 for incorrect trials, which is event code 200. Finally, after epoching, we resample the data to 128 Hertz.

For validation, we use GroupKFold-by-subject. With approximately 256 subjects and N_SPLITS set to 5, each fold holds out roughly one-fifth of the subjects—that's about 51 subjects—as the test set, while training on the remaining subjects.

Let's look at the EEG data dimension and how we can organize it. We have two main ways of structuring this data: Channel by Time, shown on the left, and Component by Time, on the right.

On the left side, we're looking at Channel by Time organization. The top panel shows results using EEGNet as our encoder architecture, while the bottom panel shows results using MLP. These are t-SNE visualizations of subject-level pooled features using a single shared model with in-sample data. The color coding here represents time, ranging from about 10 milliseconds in the darker purple regions to around 50 milliseconds in the yellow-green areas. You'll also notice that the dot size corresponds to prediction error.

On the right side, we have the same architectures - EEGNet on top and MLP on bottom - but now we're organizing the data by Component by Time instead of Channel by Time. Again, we're using the same t-SNE approach with subject-level pooled features, and the same color scheme for time and dot sizing for prediction error.

What's interesting here is how the temporal patterns emerge differently depending on whether we organize our data by channels or by components, and you can see this varies between the two encoder architectures as well.
